messages.content: Explain speculative decoding to an inference engineer, including verification, acceptance length, and failure modes.

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to explain speculative decoding to an inference engineer. This is a technical topic in LLM inference optimization. The target audience is someone who works on inference systems, so I should assume they understand:

- Autoregressive LLM inference basics
- KV caches, memory bandwidth as a bottleneck
- Batch size, GPU utilization concepts
- Token generation speed measured in tokens/second

Let me think about what speculative decoding actually is and make sure I get all the technical details right.

**Core idea:**

Standard autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: for each token generated, you do a full forward pass through the model, reading all model weights from HBM, just to produce one token. The arithmetic intensity is low (batch 1 case especially). The key insight: verifying tokens in parallel is much cheaper than generating them sequentially, because a forward pass over k tokens costs nearly the same as a forward pass over 1 token (in the memory-bound regime), since the weight reading dominates.

So the idea: use a cheap "draft" model (or some other proposal mechanism) to generate k candidate tokens autoregressively, then run the large "target" model once on all k+1 tokens (the k drafts plus the last accepted token, or rather the prefix plus drafts) in parallel to verify them all. If the draft tokens match what the target would have sampled, great — you get k+1 tokens for one target forward pass. If not, you reject and fall back.

**The crucial theoretical guarantee:** Speculative decoding with the standard rejection sampling scheme is provably lossless — the output distribution is exactly the same as sampling from the target model alone. This is important to explain carefully.

**The verification/rejection sampling scheme (Leviathan et al. 2022, Chen et al. 2023):**

Given target distribution p(x) and draft distribution q(x), for each drafted token:
- If draft sampled token x, and p(x) ≥ q(x): accept.
- Otherwise: reject, and resample from the residual distribution norm(max(p - q, 0)) = (p - q)+ / ||(p - q)+||₁.

This is the modified rejection sampling that makes the marginal distribution of accepted tokens exactly p. The intuition: the acceptance probability for token x is min(1, p(x)/q(x)), and the leftover probability mass gets redistributed to tokens where p > q.

Note: this is per-token independent rejection sampling. Important detail:
